settings.title: Flat-Fee Nil T2 Filing for E-Commerce Corporations

settings.editor:
Switching off a storefront does not switch off the corporation behind it. The seller account is deactivated, the last stock is cleared at cost or left in a spare room, and the domain renews on its own while the entity stays registered. We file the dark years at $300.00 plus HST per tax year.

Whether you sold on a marketplace, ran a direct-to-consumer brand, dropshipped, or printed on demand, we read every payout channel before treating a year as nil, carry any remaining stock or held processor balance on Schedule 100, and sign one T183CORP per year. A released balance makes that year a full return instead.

settings.title_text: A Dark Year Is Still a Tax Year
settings.description_text: Switching the store off ends the trading, not the filing. The return is what ends that.
The Agency can require the return in writing, and the notice sets a date of its own.

Every dark year goes in before the entity can be formally closed.

Most sellers either come back to it or sell what is left of it. Both depend on a corporation whose filings are current, and neither is helped by a run of dark years nobody dealt with.

Each dark year is $300.00 plus HST per tax year, filed oldest first, with any remaining stock or held processor balance carried on Schedule 100 so the figures reconcile across the run.

settings.title_text: A Processor Balance Is Still Money
settings.description_text: Funds held by a processor belong to the corporation and show on Schedule 100 until released.

settings.title_text: Unsold Stock Stays on the Books
settings.description_text: Inventory nobody has cleared is an asset. Holding it is not activity. Selling or writing it off is.

settings.title_text: Foreign Sales Do Not Change the T2
settings.description_text: Where the buyers were does not decide the return. What the corporation earned decides it.

settings.html:
The year is nil

  • No order was sold, shipped or fulfilled
  • No payment processor or marketplace released funds to the corporation
  • No remaining stock was sold, liquidated or written off
  • No refund, chargeback or dispute was settled
  • The store, domain, brand or seller account was not sold

The year is not nil

  • A processor or marketplace transferred a residual balance out
  • Leftover inventory was cleared, sold on or written down
  • A customer refund or a chargeback was settled either way
  • The domain, brand or customer list changed hands
  • An advertising rebate or platform credit reached the corporation

Due either way

  • One T2 per tax year, right up to the day the corporation is struck
  • A signed T183CORP covering each of those years
  • A closed GST/HST number, which shutting the storefront did not close
  • Any processor balance, shown on Schedule 100 until it is released
  • Proof of the last shipped order, which fixes the first dark year

settings.title: Online Store Corporation Filing Across Canada

settings.editor:
E-commerce corporations are filed the same way wherever the registered office sits, because the return is prepared and transmitted electronically from end to end. There is nothing to print, nothing to post and nothing to sign in person.

Where the corporation was incorporated changes the registry, not the return. An Ontario corporation answers to the Ontario Business Registry, and corporations in British Columbia, Alberta, Quebec and Saskatchewan each answer to their own. The T2 itself is federal and identical in all of them. Within Ontario, a corporation registered in Toronto, Mississauga, Brampton or Ottawa is filed on the same terms and at the same price as one anywhere else in the country.

Two provinces add a return the federal T2 does not cover. A Quebec corporation also files the CO-17 and an Alberta corporation also files the AT1. Both are separate provincial returns, and neither is included in the $300.00 plus HST fee.

No. A released balance is the corporation receiving its own money as revenue in that year, which makes it an ordinary return.
No. Holding inventory is not activity. It sits on Schedule 100 as an asset. Selling it, clearing it or writing it off is what ends the nil year.
No. Where the buyers were does not decide the corporate return. A Canadian corporation files a T2 on what it earned, wherever it earned it.
A cost the corporation pays is activity and takes the year out of nil. A renewal a shareholder pays personally does not.
It is a separate account with obligations of its own, and Form RC145 is what closes it. Taking the storefront offline does nothing to it.
The year of the sale, which is a disposal and so a full return. The years on either side of it can still be nil.
One authorised signing officer signs per tax year. Both founders still appear on Schedule 50 where each holds 10% or more.
Dissolution does not clear them. No clearance certificate is issued while a year is missing, and winding up adds one more T2, due six months after the dissolution date.
There is no limit. Every outstanding year gets a T2 of its own and a T183CORP of its own, priced at $300.00 plus HST per tax year, and they go across oldest to newest.
